extracted.intended_audience: educated early-18th-century English periodical readers (Spectator readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Short, didactic periodical essays remarking on social conduct, private morals, and manners (topics include justice in narrative, sexual and political vice, recommendation-letter etiquette, religious cheerfulness, and age-appropriate behaviour).

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative justice must satisfy the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: The Mind of Man is naturally a Lover of Justice, and when we read a Story wherein a Criminal is overtaken, in whom there is no Quality which is the Object of Pity, the Soul enjoys a certain Revenge for the Offence done to its Nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories in which a criminal who deserves no pity is ultimately overtaken provide moral satisfaction to readers; the included Sapphira–Rhynsault narrative is offered as an exemplifying case (villainous governor coerces and murders; public retribution follows).

rubrics_metrics.name: Condemnation of abuse of power and sexual coercion
rubrics_metrics.description: The governor (Rhynsault) imprisons a husband on false pretence to compel the wife, violates her, then executes the husband—such conduct is presented as brutal, unpitying, and morally odious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abuse of political authority to gratify lust and subvert justice is a grave vice; exemplary retribution (the Duke forcing restitution and then executing the governor) is portrayed as proper remedy and moral lesson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation-letter etiquette (Horace model)
rubrics_metrics.description: A good recommendation shows 'a slowness to ask a Favour, a strong Reason for being unable to deny his good Word any longer, and that it is a Service to the Person to whom he recommends, to comply with what is asked.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations should avoid appearing as mere charity; they should include modest hesitation to ask, a compelling reason why the recommender now must speak, and make compliance useful to the recipient. The Horace translation is provided as an ideal model of form and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honest and discriminating references — avoid passing the worthless
rubrics_metrics.description: There is nothing a Man should be more ashamed of, than passing a worthless Creature into the Service or Interests of a Man who has never injured you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good-breeding and politeness often lead people to give unjust positive testimonials; recommenders should not smooth over faults or supply dishonest credentials. Concrete examples (undertakers who fabricate recommendations; Jack Toper's candid note about a servant) illustrate honest, context-aware reference-giving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence versus coquetry in attracting attention
rubrics_metrics.description: A continent (reserved) woman, though possessing equal wit and good-humour, is often less noticed than one who uses familiar airs and coquettish gestures (dancing walk, running into rooms, a pretty shiver, carrying the fan between both hands, artful sitting, out-of-breath approach, ogling, 'swingers').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation of specific outward 'airs' and small arts by coquettes explains why libertine behaviour often draws men's attention; the essay offers a taxonomy of such airs as a practical account of what wins notice in social company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategies for prudent women competing with coquettes
rubrics_metrics.description: To be observed when prudence is undervalued, one must either wage war upon the coquets or adopt their airs: 'There is no other way but to make war upon them, or we must go over to them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The correspondent (Matilda) proposes adopting the outward signs of coquetry (lisp, trip, loll, start, blush, weep agreeably) as pragmatic tactics when sober virtue is socially ignored; the text frames this as a regrettable but realistic social decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: True religion includes cheerfulness, not perpetual melancholy
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not the Business of Virtue to extirpate the Affections of the Mind... Religion contracts the Circle of our Pleasures, but leaves it wide enough for her Votaries to expatiate in... the true Spirit of Religion cheers, as well as composes the Soul; it banishes levity but fills the Mind with perpetual Serenity and habitual Inclination to please.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious piety should not be displayed as continual gloom or moroseness; writers and preachers who make religion appear unsociable deter others. The essay argues for a balanced piety that allows innocent pleasure and social cheerfulness while avoiding vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age-appropriate conduct and moderation of pleasures
rubrics_metrics.description: Ancients allotted inclinations and objects of desire particular to every stage [of life]... by maintaining a Decency and Regularity in the Course of Life, they supported the Dignity of human Nature; it is monstrous when Feebleness attempts to adorn itself with outward Pomp and Lustre proper to Youth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One should moderate behaviour and pleasures according to life stage: indulgences excused in youth are unbecoming in old age; elders flaunting youthful pomp are ridiculous. The ideal is orderly progression of manners aligned with age.
